description: This module introduces the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC), 1908, the primary procedural law governing civil courts in India. It covers foundational principles designed to prevent multiplicity of proceedings, such as Res Sub Judice and Res Judicata, and outlines the basic structure of a civil suit, including pleadings and decrees.

res_sub_judice.concept: Res Sub Judice (Section 10 - Stay of Suit)
key_points: Meaning: 'Under judgment' or a matter currently under judicial consideration.

The Rule: Section 10 of the CPC states that no court shall proceed with the trial of any suit in which the matter in issue is also directly and substantially in issue in a previously instituted suit between the same parties.
Objective: To prevent courts of concurrent jurisdiction from simultaneously entertaining two parallel litigations involving the same cause of action, thereby avoiding conflicting decisions.

The Rule: Section 11 prohibits a court from trying any suit or issue in which the matter directly and substantially in issue has already been heard and finally decided by a competent court in a former suit between the same parties.
Objective: Founded on public policy to bring an end to litigation (preventing endless lawsuits) and to protect individuals from being vexed twice for the same cause (double jeopardy in civil law).
Plaint (Order VII): The formal written statement of claim filed by the 'Plaintiff' to institute a civil suit. It contains the facts of the case and the relief claimed.
Written Statement (Order VIII): The formal reply or defense filed by the 'Defendant' in response to the plaintiff's plaint, admitting or denying the allegations.

Decree (Section 2(2)): The formal expression of an adjudication by the court which conclusively determines the rights of the parties regarding all or any of the matters in controversy. A decree can be 'preliminary' (further proceedings are needed) or 'final' (completely disposes of the suit).

questions.question: Which legal doctrine in the Code of Civil Procedure prevents the same parties from filing a fresh suit on a matter that has already been finally decided by a competent court?
questions.explanation: 'Res Judicata' (Section 11 of the CPC) translates to 'a matter judged'. It ensures finality in litigation by barring the same parties from re-litigating a case or an issue that has already been conclusively decided by a competent court.

questions.question: Ravi files a civil suit against Amit in a Delhi court regarding a property dispute. A month later, while the Delhi case is still pending, Ravi files an identical suit regarding the exact same property dispute against Amit in a Gurugram court. Under the CPC, what action must the Gurugram court take?

options.A: The Gurugram court must dismiss the Delhi court case.
options.B: The Gurugram court must try the case simultaneously to speed up justice.
options.C: The Gurugram court must stay (halt) the trial of the newly filed suit.
options.D: The Gurugram court must merge the two courts into a joint tribunal.

questions.explanation: Under the principle of 'Res Sub Judice' (Section 10 of the CPC), when two identical suits between the same parties are filed in courts of concurrent jurisdiction, the court where the subsequent (later) suit is filed must stay its proceedings to prevent parallel trials and conflicting judgments.

questions.question: In a suit for the partition of a joint family property, the court issues a decision declaring the specific shares (percentages) each family member is entitled to, but leaves the actual physical division of the property for a later stage. How is this decision legally categorized under the CPC?
questions.explanation: This is a 'Preliminary Decree'. Under Section 2(2) of the CPC, a decree is preliminary when further proceedings have to be taken before the suit can be completely disposed of. Here, the rights (shares) are determined, but the final physical partition is pending, making it a preliminary adjudication.
